self-perceived obesity was significantly associated with cardiometabolic risks and MetS in Korean adults.
self-perceived obesity, independent of actual body weight, is positively associated with cardiometabolic risks and MetS among Koreans.
self-perception (i.e., perceived overweight/obesity) is a significant risk factor for metabolic syndrome and cardiometabolic health, independent of actual body weight.

the relationship between self-perceived overweight/obesity and cardiometabolic risk among Korean adults.
the relationship between perceived obesity and metabolic syndrome in Korean adults.
the relationship between weight perception and cardiometabolic risk among Korean adults.

self-perceived obesity is an important indicator of cardiometabolism in Koreans.
the association between self-perception and cardiometabolic risk is stronger in men than in women.
the association between weight status perception and cardiometabolic health is not clear, and further research is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-perceived obesity is a risk factor for cardiometabolic health independent of actual body weight, particularly among men.
self-perceived obesity is a strong predictor of cardiometabolic risk, even after adjusting for sociodemographic and health behavior characteristics.
self-perceived obesity is associated with cardiometabolic risk among Korean adults, even when controlling for actual body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-perception may have a stronger impact than actual weight on cardiometabolic risk in Asian men.
weight status perception may be a better predictor of cardiometabolic outcomes than body weight, especially among men.
the perception of being overweight is associated with a higher risk of cardiometabolic diseases among Korean adults, regardless of actual weight.
